title: Like the bees
hookLine: gather from many flowers and make honey that is your own (Letters 84)

lines: A BEE VISITS FLOWER AFTER FLOWER.
HONEY: NONE OF THEM AND ALL OF THEM.
cards: Watch a bee on a summer afternoon. It doesn't stay on one flower: clover, lavender, a weed by the fence. What it carries home isn't a bouquet.
In the hive, something happens to all of it, and what comes out is honey, which tastes like none of the flowers and all of them. A couple of weeks ago, Seneca told Lucilius to stop only quoting.
In the eighty-fourth letter, he explains what to do instead with everything you read, and he borrows the bee to do it.

teach.h: GATHER, THEN SORT INTO THE COMB.
teach.b: We should imitate the bees, Seneca says. They wander and pick the flowers suited to making honey, then arrange and sort what they've brought into the cells of the comb.
Reading should range widely the same way, and what we gather should be sorted and blended into one flavor.

teach.h: DIGEST IT, OR IT'S JUST WEIGHT.
teach.b: Food that sits undigested in the stomach is just a weight, he says. Only when it's changed does it become strength and blood. Reading is the same: until it's digested, it sits in the memory, not in the mind.
Even if your influences show, you should resemble them the way a child resembles a parent, not the way a portrait does. A portrait is a dead copy. A child is something new with a family face.
Many voices sing together, high and low, men and women, with a flute among them, and from all of them one sound rises. That's what he wants for a mind: many sources, one voice.
It's how this path has tried to work. Epictetus, Seneca, the Psalms, Zhuangzi, a scientist, a poet: always named, never mashed into one teaching. But the honey you make from them is yours.

how: Readers on their own path often keep notes from many sources, each one credited, and then try to put what they've learned together in their own words.

o: Latin for wildflowers gathered into a single bouquet
Latin for honey, the sweet food stored for winter
Latin for bees, which gather widely and make one honey

games.q: like the bees — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca tells Lucilius to read only one author
he says to gather from many, then blend what you gather.
Seneca says your work should resemble your influences like a child, not a portrait
a family face, but something new.
for Seneca, reading you haven't digested is still a burden

games.q: you've read twenty books on how to live and can quote all of them. what does the eighty-fourth letter ask next?
o: digest them and blend them into something your own.
pick your favorite and copy it exactly.
games.why: Seneca says to imitate the bees: gather widely, then sort and blend into one honey, your own.

practice: Bring to mind two ideas from this path you've liked, from two different sources, and hold one in each hand. Let them meet: where do they touch, and what one sentence of your own would carry a bit of both?
Don't force it; let the honey take its time.

wordCard.voice: Apes. Latin for bees, which Seneca says we should imitate: gather from many flowers, digest what you gather, and make one honey, recognizably your own. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: bees. Seneca, Letters 84.3: 'apes, ut aiunt, debemus imitari', we should imitate the bees, as they say.
